title: Run your first scientific program
intro: A specimen report is a small but useful first scientific program. It teaches execution, readable metadata, units, types, errors, documentation and reproducible runs.

scientific_context.caution: HPA images are motivating context here; synthetic values are not calibrated fluorescence.

goals.title: Run a scientific Python script
goals.why: Python replaces handwritten transcription when the same program can describe another sample.
explain: Python executes statements in order. Typing a command does nothing until Run executes it.
Assignment such as sample_id = 'N2' stores a value but produces no printed output. print(sample_id) explicitly emits stdout.
A notebook may show the last expression automatically, while a script needs print. Predict output before running, then deliberately remove print to confirm.

worked_example.predict: How many lines are printed, and why?

goals.misconception: No output means the assignment did not execute.
goals.scientific_boundary: Numbers are invented training records, not biological replicate observations.

goals.title: Name experimental data with variables
goals.why: Meaningful names prevent copied scripts from silently referring to the wrong sample.
explain: Use descriptive snake_case names such as specimen_id rather than x. Text identifiers stay strings, while counts remain numerical values.
Names refer to values in the present execution namespace. After changing a name's value, statements that previously used the old value will not be recomputed automatically.
A reusable report should derive text from its inputs; changing the specimen ID must change the output without editing the string literal of the report.

worked_example.predict: If field_count is changed to 9, which expression must be rerun?

goals.misconception: A specimen identifier with digits is a numerical measurement.
goals.scientific_boundary: Fields, images and biological replicates are distinct experimental units.

goals.title: Calculate quantities and units
goals.why: Science requires dimensional meaning as well as arithmetic correctness.
explain: A pixel width can be converted to micrometres only with a verified pixel calibration. A width of 48 pixels at 4 pixels per micrometre represents 12 micrometres.
The unit relationship is pixels divided by pixels per micrometre. Multiplication would produce the wrong physical quantity, even though Python could run the expression successfully.
A larger pixels-per-micrometre value gives a smaller physical width for a fixed pixel count. Zero calibration causes ZeroDivisionError and must not be invented or silently replaced.

worked_example.code:
width_pixels = 48
pixels_per_um = 4.0
width_um = width_pixels / pixels_per_um
print(width_um)
worked_example.predict: What happens to width_um if pixels_per_um is doubled?

goals.misconception: A numerical result with no units is already scientifically meaningful.
goals.scientific_boundary: The calibration and time interval here are synthetic assumptions, not microscope metadata.

goals.title: Inspect integers, floats and Booleans
goals.why: Correct type interpretation prevents subtle errors in scientific code.
explain: Python has integers (int), floating-point numbers (float), truth values (bool), and strings (str). The string '12.5' is not yet a number.
Use type(value).__name__ to inspect a value. Division with / returns a float even for integer inputs. A numeric string must be deliberately converted using float(...).
Python treats bool as a subclass of int, but that technical detail never makes a pass/fail flag a valid continuous biological measurement.

worked_example.code:
field_count = 6
width_um = 12.5
qc_pass = True
for value in (field_count, width_um, qc_pass):
    print(type(value).__name__)
worked_example.predict: Which three type names are printed?

goals.misconception: What print displays is sufficient to identify a value's type.
goals.scientific_boundary: A Boolean QC flag is not a quantitative measurement.

goals.title: Read tracebacks and repair mistakes
goals.why: Tracebacks are diagnostic evidence; masking them threatens reproducibility.
explain: A traceback points to the statement that failed and ends with an exception class and explanation. Read the last line first, then inspect variable names on the failing line.
A NameError normally means the referenced name is undefined, often because of a typo or an execution-order problem. Correct the cause rather than hardcoding the result.
ZeroDivisionError and ValueError are different: the first indicates an invalid denominator, the second can indicate failed numeric parsing. Both deserve investigation.

worked_example.predict: Which variable name does NameError identify?

goals.misconception: An exception can be ignored if the final-looking number is plausible.
goals.scientific_boundary: Do not replace invalid calibration with an invented measurement.

goals.title: Read help and function documentation
goals.why: Documentation skills transfer across NumPy, Pandas, scikit-image and rapidly changing libraries.
explain: Built-ins such as len, abs and round have documented behavior. Many expose a __doc__ attribute that you can inspect; help(...) also opens documentation.
When approaching a function, identify its expected input, return value and failure behavior. The purpose is to understand an interface, not to memorize long documentation paragraphs.
Rounding changes displayed precision; it cannot improve the accuracy of an uncalibrated measurement. The same distinction will matter in microscopy statistics.

worked_example.predict: Does displaying two decimals make a measurement more accurate?

goals.misconception: Reading an example's output is the same as knowing its documented behavior.
goals.scientific_boundary: Formatting is not scientific calibration or measurement uncertainty.

goals.title: Understand notebook state and clean runs
goals.why: Out-of-order notebooks can produce plausible but stale numbers even without an exception.
explain: Notebook cells share interpreter state. Editing the text of an earlier cell does not rerun calculations stored in downstream variables.
In a clean script, statements execute top to bottom. To verify a notebook, restart its kernel and run all cells in the documented order.
This studio exercise simulates stale state using normal statements. It does not pretend that the browser editor already provides full Jupyter semantics; a real notebook handoff appears in P06.

worked_example.code:
field_count = 4
doubled = field_count * 2
field_count = 9
print(doubled)  # still 8
worked_example.predict: Why does doubled remain 8 after field_count becomes 9?

goals.misconception: Changing code in a previous cell automatically updates stored values.
goals.scientific_boundary: A visually plausible but stale analysis result is not reproducible.
